answers.answer: To turn Node.js compatibility off, remove the `nodejs_compat` flag from your Worker's `compatibility_flags` in `wrangler.toml` (or `wrangler.jsonc`/`wrangler.json`). Node.js compatibility is enabled by the flag itself, and since your compatibility date is after August 2026, the `nodes_compat_v2`-style behavior is also governed by the date, so you may need to set `compatibility_date` to an earlier date to fully disable it. If you have `nodejs_compat` listed, delete that entry, then run `npx wrangler deploy` to apply the change. Check the Cloudflare Workers compatibility flags docs to confirm the current behavior for your date, since I can't verify the exact date-based defaults from here.

Pass `--env <name>` to select a block defined under `[env.<name>]` in `wrangler.toml`, and include `--legacy-env` (or set `legacy_env = true` in the config) to use the legacy service-environment behavior:

```powershell
npx wrangler deploy --env staging --legacy-env
```

In this mode, each environment is deployed as a separate Worker, with the environment name typically appended to the base name (e.g., `my-worker-staging`). I'm not certain of the exact naming and default behavior for your Wrangler version, since Wrangler changed environment handling across v2, v3, and v4. Run `npx wrangler deploy --help` and check the Wrangler environments docs for your installed version to confirm.

Set the environment variable `WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS` to `false` before running Wrangler. On Windows PowerShell, use `$env:WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS = "false"`; on bash or zsh, use `export WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS=false`. To make it permanent on Windows, set it under System Environment Variables or run `setx WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS false` (open a new terminal afterward for it to take effect). You can also turn it off persistently with `wrangler telemetry disable`.

Use the `--jurisdiction` flag when creating the database:

```bash
npx wrangler d1 create my-database --jurisdiction eu
```

For the US, the jurisdiction value is `fedramp`, which is Cloudflare's US-restricted jurisdiction. Note that D1 jurisdictions are set at creation time and can't be changed later, so you'll need to recreate the database to move it. You can also set it in `wrangler.toml` or `wrangler.jsonc` via the `jurisdiction` key under `[[d1_databases]]`.

In local `wrangler dev`, `console.log` output and runtime errors print to your terminal and aren't sent to Cloudflare. If you run with `--remote`, requests execute on Cloudflare's network, and logs go to your Cloudflare dashboard or `wrangler tail` instead. Wrangler's own anonymized usage telemetry is separate from these logs, and you can turn it off with `wrangler telemetry disable` or by setting `WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS=false`. To stop Cloudflare from storing logs for deployed Workers, set `enabled = false` under `[observability]` in `wrangler.toml`. I haven't checked these against the current docs for your Wrangler version, so confirm the exact command names with `wrangler --help` or the docs.

Not as a built-in setting that I know of. Wrangler doesn't offer a per-object delay, and existing Durable Object instances generally pick up new code when they next restart, which can be right after deploy. If you need old and new code to coexist, the usual workarounds are to give the new behavior a new class name with a migration, so old instances keep running the old class, or to version the logic inside the object's state and branch on it. Cloudflare's docs on Durable Object migrations and gradual deployments are the place to confirm the current behavior, since this area changes.

Cloudflare Workflows don't have a built-in "max concurrency" setting, so you cap concurrency in your own code. The usual approaches are to limit how many instances you create at once (for example, by using a Queue with `max_concurrency` on the consumer, then calling `env.MY_WORKFLOW.create()` from the consumer), or to check a counter in a Durable Object or KV before creating a new instance and decrement it when each instance finishes. If you need a hard cap on instances running at once, the Queue approach is the simplest, since the queue consumer's `max_concurrency` setting limits how many batches are processed in parallel. Check the current Workflows docs for the exact config keys, since they may have changed.

Yes, but not with a plain Cloudflare Worker. Workers handle HTTP(S) and WebSocket traffic, so they can't bind to port 5432 or act as a general TCP listener. Cloudflare's **TCP sockets API** (`cloudflare:sockets`, `connect()`) lets a Worker make outbound raw TCP connections, which is how a Worker can talk to a Postgres server, but it can't accept inbound TCP. For a Postgres proxy that listens on 5432, you'd need to run it on a server or container (for example, a VM or Cloudflare Containers) and use a Worker only as an HTTP or WebSocket front end.

Use `wrangler versions secret delete <SECRET_NAME>` instead of `bulk`. `versions secret bulk` only adds or updates the secrets in the JSON file you pass it, so it can't remove one. The delete command creates a new version without that secret, and you still need to deploy that version (for example, with `wrangler versions deploy`) before it takes effect. A scheduled callback receives the **payload** you passed when you created the schedule, as its single argument. In the Cloudflare Agents SDK, you call `this.schedule(when, "methodName", payload)`, and the SDK invokes that method on the agent with `payload` when the time comes. The payload should be serializable, such as a JSON-compatible object or string. If you omit it, the callback gets `undefined`. I haven't checked this against the current SDK source, so confirm the exact signature in the Cloudflare docs if your version differs.

The first message is a JSON-RPC `initialize` request from the client to the server. It carries the client's supported `protocolVersion`, its `capabilities`, and `clientInfo` (name and version). The server replies with its own protocol version and capabilities, and the client then sends a `notifications/initialized` notification before any other requests. Cloudflare's Agents SDK uses the standard MCP TypeScript SDK, so this follows the MCP spec. Over Streamable HTTP, the server may also return an `Mcp-Session-Id` header that the client includes on later requests.

The test passes even if the promise resolves to the wrong value. Vitest doesn't wait for the un-awaited assertion, so the test function finishes first. If the assertion later fails, the rejection surfaces as an unhandled rejection, which Vitest reports as an error, often attributed to the wrong test or to the run as a whole. Fix it with `await expect(promise).resolves.toBe(1)` or by returning the assertion. The `vitest/valid-expect` ESLint rule catches this pattern.

No, Vitest won't pick up a `vitest.config.ts` from a parent directory. It looks for the config in the current working directory (the project root), and if none is found it falls back to `vite.config.*` there, so running from a subfolder with no config will use default settings.

To use a parent config, pass it explicitly: `npx vitest --config ../vitest.config.ts --root ..`. Alternatively, run Vitest from the directory that contains the config.

Usually not. If you're running tests with Vitest, import the APIs from `vitest` itself, since it re-exports what you need. Add `@vitest/runner` only if you're building a custom runner or using its APIs without the full Vitest package. In that case, add it as a devDependency pinned to the same version as `vitest`, because mismatched versions can cause subtle failures. Yes. In `@testing-library/jest-dom`'s `toHaveTextContent`, a string argument is matched as a substring of the element's normalized text content, so `expect(el).toHaveTextContent('world')` passes for `

hello world

`. Whitespace is normalized before comparison by default. If you need an exact match, pass a regular expression with anchors (e.g., `/^hello world$/`) or use `toHaveTextContent` with the `normalizeWhitespace` option set to `false` and an exact pattern.

By default, `--reporter=blob` writes its output to a `.vitest-reports/` directory in the project root, with file names that include the shard index (for example, `blob-1-3.json` for shard 1 of 3). You can change the location with the `outputFile` option. I haven't checked this against the Vitest version installed here, so confirm it with `npx vitest --help` or the docs for your version.

In Vitest, `-t` (or `--testNamePattern`) matches against the full name, which joins every enclosing `describe` title with the test title by spaces. So you pass the whole chain, or a regex that matches it. For example, `npx vitest run -t "MyComponent handles empty input"` runs only the test `handles empty input` inside `describe("MyComponent")`. You can also use a looser regex like `-t "handles empty input"`, which matches any test with that substring. Since `-t` is a regex, escape special characters such as parentheses. On Windows PowerShell, quote the argument with double quotes, as shown above.

Yes. Vitest browser-mode locators such as `getByText` follow Playwright's semantics, so they match substrings and ignore case by default. Pass `{ exact: true }` to require a full, case-sensitive match of the element's text. Because a partial match can hit more than one element, a strict locator will throw if it matches multiple elements, so use `exact: true` or a more specific query when you need one.

`expect.poll` keeps calling the function and re-checking the assertion until it passes or the timeout expires (Playwright's default is 5 seconds, configurable with the `timeout` option). If the timeout expires, the assertion fails and the test errors, reporting the last value the function returned or the last error it threw.

No, not in the usual sense. Vitest hoists `vi.mock` calls to the top of their file, before imports, so calling it inside a function or `if` block won't behave as you'd expect. Only the calls at the top level of the module are reliably hoisted and applied. If you need conditional mocking, use `vi.doMock`, which isn't hoisted and applies to subsequent dynamic `import()` calls, or use `vi.hoisted` for values the mock factory needs. Either way, the mock factory itself can't reference variables declared outside it unless they're created with `vi.hoisted`.

No, not by default. Inline projects in `test.projects` are configured independently, so options set in the root config's `test` block don't carry over to them. To inherit the root configuration, set `extends: true` on the inline project. I'm answering from memory of the Vitest docs, so check the `test.projects` section for your installed version if the behavior matters for your setup.

Vitest doesn't have a built-in "repeat N times" flag, so the usual approach is a loop in the shell. In PowerShell, run `for ($i = 1; $i -le 20; $i++) { npx vitest run path/to/flaky.test.ts; if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { break } }`, which stops at the first failure so you can inspect it. Alternatively, `vitest run --sequence.shuffle` randomizes test order within a run, which often surfaces order-dependent flakiness, and `--sequence.seed=<n>` makes a failing order reproducible. For a single test, you can also use `-t "test name"` to narrow the loop to just that test. If you want Vitest to repeat a test in one process, `test.repeats` (available in newer versions) is another option, but the shell loop is the most reliable way to catch flakiness across independent runs.

I don't believe Vitest defines a short alias for `--project`. You pass it in full, and it can be repeated to run several projects, e.g. `vitest --project unit --project e2e`. Running `npx vitest --help` in your project will confirm the flags for your installed version.

Yes, `vitest list` imports your test files to collect the tests, but it doesn't execute the test bodies, hooks, or assertions. Top-level code in those files does run during import, and `describe` callbacks run because they define the tests. Test bodies don't run, so no assertions execute. I'm going from memory of Vitest's behavior, so check the docs for your installed version if the exact semantics matter.
